title: Smuck v. Hobson (1969)
summary: The court allowed limited parental intervention to appeal school-decree provisions while distinguishing the positions of individual officials.
notes:
The syllabus requires reading this material but states that class time will not be spent on intervention. The entry remains in the reading universe and is labeled accordingly in Week 12.

The underlying case was Hobson v. Hansen, in which Judge J. Skelly Wright found the D.C. schools' tracking system and other practices discriminated against black and poor children; the D.C. Circuit decided Smuck en banc in an opinion by Judge Bazelon, denying intervention to former superintendent Carl Hansen and dissenting board member Carl Smuck but allowing twenty parents to intervene and appeal only the decree provisions restricting the board's future discretion.

sections.Parties: Parents and school officials sought to participate after a decree concerning the District of Columbia school system.
sections.Material Facts: The litigation challenged discriminatory features of the school system, including tracking and other arrangements. After judgment, the school board declined to appeal. Some parents asserted interests in educational choices and school policies affected by the decree. A former superintendent and an individual board member also sought review, but their asserted interests differed from the parents’ interests.
sections.Procedural History: The appellate court considered intervention and authority to pursue an appeal after the board’s decision. It permitted parental intervention within a limited scope.
sections.Issue: Could the parents intervene to protect interests they believed the school board no longer adequately represented?
sections.Holding: Yes with limits directed to the relevant provisions of the decree. The other applicants’ official history or disagreement did not automatically entitle them to appeal.
sections.Reasoning: Intervention required an interest that might be impaired and a showing that existing representation might be inadequate. The board had public responsibilities broader than those of a particular group of parents, so its decision against appeal did not necessarily represent their interests. The court confined intervention to the matters genuinely affecting those interests. It separately rejected reliance on reputational concerns or a single board member’s disagreement as an independent basis to control the litigation.

learning.why: The court allowed limited parental intervention to appeal school-decree provisions while distinguishing the positions of individual officials.

topics.cp-intervention: Parents could intervene for a limited appeal when the school board declined to appeal and their interests might be inadequately represented.
topics.cp-adequate-representation: A government body’s wider responsibilities can differ from the interests of a particular group.
topics.cp-party-status: A former official’s reputation or a board member’s disagreement did not alone establish a personal right to appeal.
topics.cp-judicial-discretion: Smuck permits intervention to protect the parents’ interest while limiting the scope of their participation to that interest.
topics.cp-frcp-24: The court parsed each Rule 24(a)(2) element (interest, impairment, adequate representation) for three different sets of applicants.

mnemonic.rationale: Parents who wanted to appeal the school case
